promoted: {rival}, your batchmate and your rival for every promotion, is promoted to {title}. The email announcing it is copied to you too, as a courtesy.
{rival}, your batchmate, is now {title}. The group chat from your first year hears about it before you do.
{rival}, your batchmate, makes {title}. {They} sent round a very nice message, which you have read twice.
This year's promotions go out in an HR circular, in alphabetical order. {rival}, your batchmate, is on it as {title}, and three people forward it to you, in case you missed it.

{rival}, your batchmate, is promoted to {title}. The drinks stall auntie downstairs, who has known you both since your first year, hears before you do, and makes your coffee a little sweeter without being asked.
{rival}, your batchmate, is promoted to {title} and moves into an office with a door. {rival} tells everyone the door will always be open. It is, whenever you walk past.
{rival}, your batchmate, becomes {title}. Your intake's yearly dinner moves to a nicer restaurant this time, and {rival} is the one who picks it.
{rival}, your batchmate, is promoted to {title}, and the new business cards arrive within the week. {rival} gives you one, which no colleague has ever done before.

The promotions are announced at the ministry's town hall, one slide per name. {rival}, your batchmate, gets a slide as {title}, with a photograph from a retreat at which you were also present, just out of frame.
winService: This year there was one promotion slot at your grade, and two of you up for it: you and {rival}, your batchmate and your rival for every promotion. It went to you, and {rival} congratulated you within the minute, so the news must have reached {them} first.
The promotion panel could take only one of you at this grade, and it took you. {rival}, your batchmate, took it well, in the sense that nobody saw {them} take it.

The promotion panel had one slot at your grade and two names from the same intake: yours and that of {rival}, your batchmate. Yours went up. The next morning there is a cake on your desk from the good bakery, with no card, and you know exactly who sent it.

This year's promotions had room for one of the two of you, and the panel chose you over {rival}, your batchmate. Years ago you agreed that whoever lost would buy the coffee, and {rival} remembers, to the cent.

Only one of you could go up this year, you or {rival}, your batchmate, and the panel picked you. {rival} found out from the HR system before you did, and messaged you a single thumbs-up, which you have looked at more than once.

One slot, two officers from the same intake: you and {rival}, your batchmate. You got it. That evening {rival} posts a photograph of a long run round the reservoir, at a pace that is clearly a statement.

The panel could put one of you forward this year, you or {rival}, your batchmate, and put you forward. {rival}'s reporting officer tells {them} it was "a matter of timing", a phrase you will one day hear yourself.

There was room to promote one of you this year, you or {rival}, your batchmate, and it was you. At the next intake gathering {rival} raises a glass to you first, before anyone else can, and makes it sound like a favour.
loseService: There was one promotion slot at your grade this year, with you and {rival}, your batchmate and your rival for every promotion, both up for it, and it went to {rival}. You're told it was "very close". That is what everyone is told, probably including {rival}.
The panel had room for one promotion at your grade, and gave it to {rival}, your batchmate. HR says you are "next in line", and doesn't say for what.
The one promotion at your grade this year went to {rival}, your batchmate, and not to you. {rival} asks you to lunch the same week, and insists on paying, which is worse.
You and {rival}, your batchmate, were up for the same slot this year, and the panel chose {rival}. HR's note to everyone else calls the field "exceptionally strong", and you are part of the field.

This year's promotion round could move one of the two of you up, and it moved {rival}, your batchmate. Somebody has already redone the seating plan for the division retreat, and you are one table further from the front.

Only one of you could go up this year, and the panel chose {rival}, your batchmate, over you. {rival} sends you the slides from {their} promotion interview, "in case they help next time". They do, annoyingly.
winPolitics: There was one appointment open at your level this year, and the choice was between you and {rival}, your batchmate, and it went to you. {rival} was the first to shake your hand at the swearing-in, and held it a beat longer than necessary.

The Prime Minister had room to move one of you up this year, you or {rival}, your batchmate, and chose you. {rival} sends flowers to your office with a card that says "Finally", which could be about either of you.

{rival}, your batchmate, was the other name for the one appointment open at your level this year, and it went to you. In Parliament the next week, {rival} asks the first question about your new portfolio, very politely, with a follow-up ready.

When the appointments were decided, it was you or {rival}, your batchmate, and it was you. {rival} writes a note of congratulations on the party's notepaper and signs it with {their} full name, which {rival} has not done since your first week.

The appointments this year had room for one of you, you or {rival}, your batchmate, and the room was yours. {rival} heard the news on a walkabout, in front of residents, and smiled through every block.

It came down to you or {rival}, your batchmate, for the one office open at your level, and it went to you. Within the week {rival} has volunteered for three committees, and is clearly not planning to lose twice.

When the appointments were settled, your name was on the list and that of {rival}, your batchmate, was not. {rival} tells reporters the party has "a deep bench", and manages to make it sound like a compliment to you.
losePolitics: The one appointment open at your level this year went to {rival}, your batchmate, and not to you. The Prime Minister's Office describes the decision as "finely balanced".
The Prime Minister could move one of you up this year, you or {rival}, your batchmate, and moved {rival}. Your volunteers take it harder than you do, and say so, at length, over supper.

When the appointments came out, {rival}, your batchmate, had the one you had both been in line for. {rival} tells you, privately, that you would have been better at it, and seems to mean it, which does not help.
pm: {rival}, your batchmate, is to be the next Prime Minister. {They} telephoned you before the announcement, or said {they} did.
pmBlocked: The one job above yours is taken. {rival}, your batchmate, is Prime Minister, and shows no sign of having considered the private sector.
The one job above yours belongs to {rival}, your batchmate, who is Prime Minister and has just announced a ten-year plan. You are choosing to read it as a policy document.
elected: {rival}, your batchmate, was introduced at a press conference as a new candidate for Parliament, and won, and is now a Member of Parliament.
lostSeat: {rival}, your batchmate, ran for Parliament and lost the ward. A month later {rival} was back in the service at the same grade, which everyone agreed to call a homecoming.
consultancy: {rival}, your batchmate, is leaving the service for the private sector. The farewell lunch is at a hotel, so the new package must be very good.
scandal: {rival}, your batchmate, has resigned, for personal reasons. Everyone has a theory. Nobody says it in the lift.
rankedBelowService: The promotion panel put {rival}, your batchmate and your rival for every promotion, ahead of you this year. Neither of you went up: the slot went to someone from another division whom you have never met.
You were placed just below {rival}, your batchmate, this year, and neither of you was promoted. It is the one comparison everyone on the floor made, and nobody made out loud.

This year's promotion panel put {rival}, your batchmate, one place above you, and then promoted neither of you. Over lunch the two of you agree that these lists mean nothing. {rival} agrees a little more easily.

Nobody at your grade went up this year, but the panel's list still had an order, and in it {rival}, your batchmate, came just before you. The order is confidential, and by Friday the whole floor knows it.
The panel promoted neither you nor {rival}, your batchmate, but put {rival} first. The difference between first and second, you are told, is "not material", and it is written down in ink.
rankedBelowPolitics: When the appointments were settled, the name of {rival}, your batchmate, was ahead of yours on the list. Neither of you moved. Someone with no government job at all did.

Neither you nor {rival}, your batchmate, moved up when this year's appointments came out, but every newspaper that guessed at them beforehand put {rival} ahead of you. The newspapers were wrong about everything else, which is no comfort.

The party's leadership weighed you and {rival}, your batchmate, for the next appointment, put {rival} a little higher, and then gave it to neither of you. Nobody tells you this. Someone at party headquarters mentions it by accident, and asks you to forget it.

This year's appointments passed over you and {rival}, your batchmate, but {rival} was apparently the nearer miss. {rival} is asked to brief the Prime Minister on something minor, and three different people tell you about the briefing.

You and {rival}, your batchmate, were both considered for higher office this year, and neither of you got it, though {rival} came closer. The party newsletter runs {their} photograph slightly larger than yours, by about a centimetre, which you measured.

Nobody from your intake was appointed this year, but the talk in the Members' room is that {rival}, your batchmate, came closer than you. The talk in the Members' room is usually right, and never written down.
appointed: {rival}, your batchmate, is appointed {title}. The swearing-in photograph is on the front page, and you are in the background of it.
{rival}, your batchmate, is appointed {title}. The Prime Minister's press conference runs to forty minutes, and {rival}'s name comes up in the thirty-first.
The new appointments are announced on a weekday evening. {rival}, your batchmate, becomes {title}, and your phone fills with messages asking how you feel, which is how you find out.
{rival}, your batchmate, becomes {title}. {Their} first speech in the role quotes a line from your first course in the service, and {rival} looks straight at you while saying it.
{rival}, your batchmate, is appointed {title}. The papers run a profile headed "One to watch", with a photograph from {their} first year in the service, in which you appear as an elbow.
{rival}, your batchmate, becomes {title}. The party sends round a card of congratulations for every Member to sign, and it reaches you last, with just enough room at the bottom for your name.
{rival}, your batchmate, is named {title}. The flower stands outside {their} office run the length of the corridor, and the one from your volunteers is the tallest, which they made sure of.
{rival}, your batchmate, is appointed {title}, with a car, a press secretary and a diary that other people now keep. {rival} still answers your messages personally, though now at 1am.
{rival}, your batchmate, becomes {title}. At the next party dinner the two of you are seated together, by someone who thought it would be a nice touch.
promotedApart: {rival}, your batchmate, is now {title}. You hear about it at a dinner, from someone who assumes you already knew.
{rival}, your batchmate, is now {title}, and announces it online in four modest lines. Three hundred people like it within the hour, and you are the three hundred and first, so as not to seem eager.

Your paths have not crossed at work in years, so the news comes from a friend you both have: {rival}, your batchmate, is now {title}. The friend adds that {rival} asked after you, which you choose to believe.
{rival}, your batchmate, becomes {title}. You are on different ladders now, so nobody compares the two of you, out loud.

{rival}, your batchmate, is now {title}. The news reaches you on a Saturday, between a wedding dinner and a funeral wake, and at both someone asks you to pass on their congratulations, as if you saw {rival} every day.
{rival}, your batchmate, is now {title}. When you call to say well done, {rival} asks about your own work first, for ten minutes, which is either kindness or practice.
You read it in the papers first: {rival}, your batchmate, is now {title}. You send a message, and the reply comes back within the minute, which tells you {rival} had been waiting for it.
{rival}, your batchmate, has become {title}. At the next reunion of your intake the seating plan puts the two of you side by side, by someone who meant well.
{rival}, your batchmate, is now {title}. Your old canteen still has a photograph of your intake on its wall, and someone has drawn a small star next to {rival}'s face.
electedTogether: {rival}, your batchmate, stood at the same general election, in another constituency, and won, and is now a Member of Parliament too.
lostSeatTogether: {rival}, your batchmate, stood at the same general election, in another constituency, and lost. Within the month {rival} was back at {their} old desk in the service, and the division held a welcome-back lunch that nobody called a consolation.
consultancyPolitics: {rival}, your batchmate, has left Parliament for a seat on a company's board. The papers call it "an orderly transition". They call all of them that.
scandalPolitics: {rival}, your batchmate, has resigned from Parliament, for personal reasons. In the Members' room the theories are many, and every one of them is whispered.
retired: {rival}, your batchmate, retires as {title}. At the farewell lunch, {rival}'s speech thanks "my batchmate, {player.given}". You send a card afterwards, and mean it.

folder.item: a peer assessment of {rival} that did you more good than it did {them}

events.title: The 360
events.body: It's 360-degree feedback season, when colleagues assess each other anonymously and the ranking panel reads the results. You've been asked to assess {rival}, your batchmate and your rival for every promotion. The form promises anonymity. It has a free-text box headed "Areas for development".

choices.outcome: Three sentences on stakeholder management, true and mildly painful. {rival} acts on all three within a year and never learns where they came from.
It is accurate. It is also the only peer comment the ranking panel quotes. {rival} is described that year as "still developing", which you did not write but did cause.
The form accepts it. HR's report later notes "limited peer input" for your whole division. Your blank form is one of the reasons.

events.title: Annex B
events.body: {rival}, your batchmate and your rival for every promotion, sends a paper up to the Permanent Secretary at nine tomorrow, and you're copied on the draft. Annex B has the right numbers in the wrong columns, and the recommendation rests on them. A mistake like that would cost {rival} at the next ranking.

choices.outcome: {rival} fixes it at 11:50pm and says thank you twice, the second time in a voice you have not heard before.

choices.text: Say nothing. It is not your paper.
choices.outcome: The Permanent Secretary finds Annex B in four minutes. For the rest of the year {rival} is described as "detail-light". You are described as nothing at all, which this year is better.

choices.text: Raise it at the meeting, helpfully.
choices.outcome: You are thanked for your rigour. {rival} thanks you too, later, in the corridor, in a tone the minutes would not have captured.

events.title: One Posting
events.body: There's one two-year posting to the Budget Division at the Ministry of Finance this year, the kind that gets people noticed, and your division has two nominees: you and {rival}, your batchmate. HR suggests the two of you "have a conversation" first. In HR, that means one of you should withdraw.

choices.text: Withdraw, and say it was your idea.
choices.outcome: {rival} goes to Finance. Three weeks later a photograph arrives of the view from {their} new office. It is, admittedly, a very good view.

choices.text: Let HR decide on the files.

contest.winText: The posting goes to you. {rival} says {they} had expected it to, which may even be true.
contest.loseText: The posting goes to {rival}. HR's email to you uses the phrase "many strong candidates". There were two.

choices.outcome: HR decides on the files, which takes six weeks and a matrix.

choices.text: Make your case to the Director, privately.

contest.winText: The posting goes to you. {rival} hears, eventually, how.
contest.loseText: The posting goes to {rival}. The Director mentions, in passing, that {rival} did not come asking.

choices.outcome: The Director listens, nods, and promises to "bear it in mind". That is the most anyone has ever got out of that office.

events.title: Views Are Sought
events.body: {rival}, your batchmate, has been shortlisted for a post one grade above you both, which would make {rival} senior to you. The selection panel has asked {rival}'s peers for their views. Yours will be read, and filed, and remembered by someone.

choices.outcome: You write half a page and mean all of it. Someone on the panel later shows it to {rival}, who never mentions it to you and never forgets it.
Two lines, both true, neither memorable. The panel files them with the others.

choices.text: Suggest, carefully, that another year in the grade might help {them}.
choices.outcome: The panel finds your view "balanced". {rival} learns of it eventually, the way everyone here learns everything: from someone who was not supposed to say.

events.title: Saturday
events.body: {rival}, your batchmate, is an MP too, and {rival}'s ward has had a difficult year: a lift upgrading that overran, and an angry letter in the newspaper every week. {They} asked you to walk the ward with {them} on Saturday morning. Your own ward has a walkabout planned for the same morning.

choices.outcome: Six blocks, two markets, and one auntie who assumes you are {rival}'s campaign manager and tells you exactly what she thinks of {them}. The letters to the newspaper stop by March. The last one thanks "the MP from the next ward, {player.formal}".
Your volunteers are better at it than you are. {rival} thanks them by name, which you notice.
Your ward is pleased to see you. {rival} manages without you, and remembers the Saturday.

events.title: First Among Equals
events.body: Who becomes the next Prime Minister, first among equals, is being settled informally by the Cabinet, in a room. It has come down to two names, as the officers you joined with joked it would at your first dinner together: {player.given} and {rival}.

choices.outcome: You say it plainly, to the people who need to hear it. {rival} says it too, in the next room. It will be decided the way these things are: slowly, and then all at once.
{rival} thanks you once, in private, and never again. That is how you know the deal was understood.

events.title: The Name Put Forward
events.body: {rival}, your batchmate and now senior to you, has been asked to nominate officers for a cross-ministry task force. Everyone understands it is where future leaders get tested. {They} put your name first.

choices.outcome: Lunch, on you, at a place {rival} chose. It was more expensive than {they} let on, and worth it.

choices.text: Decline. You would rather go up on your own file.
choices.outcome: {rival} says that is fair. It is, and it costs you a year.
